artiest/run-dmc-en-aerosmith.text:
Run-DMC was an American hip hop group from Hollis, Queens, in New York. Joseph Simmons, Darryl McDaniels and Jason Mizell began working together in 1983. Simmons first became known as DJ Run, the DJ of the rapper Kurtis Blow, McDaniels, as Easy D, mostly sat writing rhymes on paper, and Mizell spun records as Jam Master Jay. The group's name combines the name Run with the initials of McDaniels. After signing with Profile Records, the group released its first pair of singles, It's Like That and Sucker MCs, at the end of 1983. In 1984 came the debut album Run-D.M.C., the first gold record for a hip hop group, and in 1985 King of Rock, the first platinum one. Rock Box already shows how they mixed hard hip hop with hard rock.

Raising Hell, released in 1986, became the first hip hop album to go platinum more than once. It includes Walk This Way, a reworking of the song by the American hard rock band Aerosmith from Boston, whose singer Steven Tyler and guitarist Joe Perry took part in the recording themselves. With it, Run-DMC climbed higher in the Billboard Hot 100 than Aerosmith's original ever had, reaching number four. It became one of the best-known songs in both hip hop and rock, and brought the two worlds together.

Run-DMC also abandoned the glamorous clothing of old-school hip hop and chose the street instead: black hats, jackets and Adidas without laces. They were the first hip hop group to appear in videos on MTV and on the cover of Rolling Stone. In 2009 they were inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame. Together with Aerosmith, they showed that hip hop and rock could strengthen each other.
artiest/run-dmc-en-aerosmith.listen: Listen to Walk This Way and notice the guitar riff, which comes from rock, and the rhythmic raps that leap over it. Can you hear how the voices of the rappers and of Steven Tyler take turns?

artiest/rundfunk-sinfonieorchester-berli.text:
The Rundfunk-Sinfonieorchester Berlin, known in English as the Berlin Radio Symphony Orchestra, is a German symphony orchestra. It was founded in 1923 as a radio orchestra and is regarded as the second-oldest radio orchestra, with 114 musicians. It plays in Berlin at the Konzerthaus and the Philharmonie, and in other German cities as well.

In its early years the orchestra was known for its work with contemporary composers. Guest conductors included Paul Hindemith, Arthur Honegger, Darius Milhaud, Sergei Prokofiev, Richard Strauss, Arnold Schönberg and Igor Stravinsky. The first principal conductor was Bruno Seidler-Winkler, from 1926 to 1932. The first concert after the war took place on 18 May 1945. After the division of Germany in 1949 the orchestra came under the radio service of the GDR. Since 1994 it has belonged to a joint organisation of four Berlin radio ensembles.

Later principal conductors included Sergiu Celibidache, Heinz Rögner, Rafael Frühbeck de Burgos and Marek Janowski. With Janowski the orchestra recorded ten operas by Richard Wagner for Pentatone. Since 2017 Vladimir Jurowski has been principal conductor, and his contract runs until 2027. From the 1950s to the 1980s the orchestra made recordings for Eterna, and later worked for labels including Hyperion and CPO. It remains an important home for new and lesser-known music.
artiest/rundfunk-sinfonieorchester-berli.listen: Listen to a recording of the orchestra playing twentieth-century music, for instance Bartók or Lutosławski. Notice how clearly the instrumental groups sound.

artiest/rune-carlsson.text:
Rune Carlsson is a drummer who can be heard on the album One Long String by the trio of the American jazz bassist Red Mitchell. The album was recorded in Paris in 1969 and released on the Mercury label. Besides Mitchell on bass, the Swedish pianist Bobo Stenson plays on it. Carlsson completes the trio on drums.

One Long String contains eight pieces. Mitchell wrote most of them himself, including the title track, Peggy, Undertow and Total Tumult. The album also includes Stella by Starlight, Narbild by F. Sjöström and Pojken I Grottan by Stenson. The Allmusic reviewer calls the record full of energy and daring, with a soulful undertone, and writes that, despite all the technique, the recording retains its focus and its collaborative spirit.

The album shows how Swedish and American jazz musicians worked together in Europe. Little about Carlsson's later career can be found in the available source. His role on this record is that of the rhythmic engine of a trio in which bass and piano give each other a great deal of space.
artiest/rune-carlsson.listen: Listen to the title track One Long String and focus on the drums. Notice how Carlsson supports the interplay between bass and piano without drowning it out.

artiest/rupert-gregson-williams.text:
Rupert Gregson-Williams was born in Chichester in 1966 and is an English composer, conductor and music producer, best known for film and television music. He was educated at a choir school, Lancing College and St John's College, Cambridge. He is the younger brother of the film composer Harry Gregson-Williams and a member of the team of composers at Hans Zimmer's Remote Control Productions.

His film music is wide-ranging. For Hotel Rwanda he received the European Film Award for composers. He also wrote the music for Hacksaw Ridge, Wonder Woman, Aquaman and its sequel, Over the Hedge, Bee Movie, Abominable, Back to the Outback, Made of Honor, The Holiday and The Legend of Tarzan. With Click he began a long collaboration with Adam Sandler, and he composed for many films from Sandler's production company Happy Madison. He has also written music for video games.

He was nominated twice for a Primetime Emmy Award and also received a BMI Award. His work belongs to the tradition of great orchestral Hollywood music, in which themes and a large orchestra carry the emotion of the images, and shows how film music is nowadays often made by teams working around a studio such as Zimmer's.
artiest/rupert-gregson-williams.listen: Listen to the music of Wonder Woman or Hacksaw Ridge and notice how the orchestra builds the atmosphere. Where do you hear a theme return?

artiest/rush.text:
Rush is a Canadian rock band from Toronto. The group formed in 1968 in the Willowdale district, around guitarist Alex Lifeson and drummer John Rutsey. Geddy Lee soon took the place of the first bassist and singer. In 1974, four months after the debut album Rush, Neil Peart replaced the drummer Rutsey. That completed the classic trio, which stayed together until 2015. Peart then retired from music, and in 2018 Lifeson confirmed that the band had stopped.

The group started out with blues-tinged hard rock and moved on to progressive rock. The albums 2112 from 1976, A Farewell to Kings and Hemispheres stand for that phase. From Permanent Waves and Moving Pictures in 1980 and 1981 the songs sounded shorter and tighter. In the 1980s synthesizers took on a major role, notably on Signals, Grace Under Pressure and Power Windows. Later the group returned to guitar rock, up to and including Clockwork Angels in 2012. The lyrics deal with science fiction, fantasy and philosophy.

Rush is known for virtuoso playing and complex compositions. In readers' polls of music magazines the three members won many awards as instrumentalists. The group entered the Canadian Music Hall of Fame in 1994 and the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2013. In the course the trio keeps progressive rock alive, at a time when punk and new wave dominated the picture.
artiest/rush.listen: Listen to Tom Sawyer from the album Moving Pictures and notice the drums and the synthesizer alongside the guitar. Can you hear how three people make such a full, intricate sound?

artiest/russ-winstanley.text:
Russ Winstanley was born in 1952 in Beech Hill, a district of Wigan in Lancashire. He is an English DJ, best known as a champion of northern soul at the Wigan Casino. He attended Wigan Grammar School.

On 23 September 1973 he came up with the Soul Allnighters at the Wigan Casino, where he also played records himself. They were nights that lasted until the morning and ran four evenings a week until the closure on 6 December 1981. More than four million people came through the doors. Both the Wigan Casino and Winstanley won many awards as best club and best DJ. Northern soul is the name for the fast, rhythmic soul records from America that found a second life in the dance clubs of northern England.

Even after the closure Winstanley remained active on the northern soul circuit and on the radio. He had his own programmes on BBC GMR and XFM in Manchester and has a regular northern soul programme on BBC Radio Lancashire. In 1997 he compiled the album Soul Survivors for Telstar Records. In 1998 his book Wigan Casino Story entered the bestseller list. He was also musical adviser for the production Once Upon A Time in Wigan at the Octagon in Bolton.
artiest/russ-winstanley.listen: Pick a northern soul record from the Soul Survivors collection and listen to the tempo and the drums. Could you dance to it the way the visitors in Wigan did?

artiest/rusty-egan.text:
Rusty Egan is a British-Irish musician and DJ, born in London in 1957. He began as the drummer of the new wave band Rich Kids, which existed from March 1977 to December 1978. It also featured the former Sex Pistols bassist Glen Matlock and Midge Ure. Egan continued to work with Ure and later played with, among others, The Misfits, Skids and Shock. He was also a co-founder of Visage and played drums on a remixed version of Phil Lynott's Yellow Pearl, which the BBC used as the theme tune of Top of the Pops from 1981 to 1986.

From 1979 to 1981 he spun records at Blitz, the New Romantic club in London, together with Steve Strange. There he played electronic music and synth-pop by Kraftwerk, Yellow Magic Orchestra, Eno, Ultravox and Landscape, among others, and so defined the musical style of that scene. He also had a record shop, The Cage, on King's Road. In 1981 he DJed at Croc's in Rayleigh and helped Depeche Mode get a regular night. In 1982 he, Strange and Kevin Millins opened the Camden Palace. Later he produced records for groups he had played for, such as Spear of Destiny, Shock and Visage.

Egan showed that a DJ can shape a scene, not only by choosing what is played, but also by deciding who gets to take part. In the course he appears alongside Steve Strange as the man behind the club nights where you only got in if you looked striking.
artiest/rusty-egan.listen: Listen to Fade to Grey by Visage and notice the synthesizers and the cool, spoken vocals. Can you hear how electronics from Germany end up in a London club atmosphere?

artiest/ruth-brown.text:
Ruth Brown was born in 1928 in Portsmouth, Virginia, and died in 2006. She was a singer, songwriter and actress, and was called the Queen of R&B. Her father was a dock worker and led the church choir, but Ruth preferred to sing at USO shows and in nightclubs. Her role models were Sarah Vaughan, Billie Holiday and Dinah Washington. In 1945, at the age of seventeen, she ran away from home with the trumpeter Jimmy Brown, whom she married, to sing in bars.

Blanche Calloway arranged bookings and became her manager. Through Willis Conover, later a radio presenter, she ended up at Atlantic Records, where Ahmet Ertegun persuaded her to switch from popular ballads to rhythm and blues. Her first hit was So Long, in 1949. In 1950 came Teardrops from My Eyes, which spent eleven weeks at the top of the Billboard R&B chart. Later hits included 5-10-15 Hours and (Mama) He Treats Your Daughter Mean in 1953 and Mambo Baby in 1954. She brought a pop style into R&B, and Atlantic came to be called the house that Ruth built.

From the mid-1970s she made a comeback, which peaked in the 1980s. She campaigned for musicians' rights to royalties and fair contracts, which led to the Rhythm and Blues Foundation. For her role in the Broadway musical Black and Blue she received a Tony Award. In 2016 she posthumously received a Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award.
artiest/ruth-brown.listen: Listen to Teardrops from My Eyes and notice the cheerful tempo set against the lyrics about sorrow. Can you hear how her voice sounds playful and yet sharp?

artiest/ruud-jacobs.text:
Ruud Jacobs was born in 1938 in Hilversum and died in 2019 in Nieuwkoop. He was a Dutch double bassist and producer and the younger brother of the pianist Pim Jacobs. The brothers grew up in an artistic family, with a father who was an amateur pianist and a mother who taught ballet. Ruud began on the recorder at the age of eleven and within a few months was playing compositions by Charlie Parker. At thirteen he took up the alto saxophone, later the tenor saxophone, and at fifteen the double bass. He studied for four years at the Conservatorium van Amsterdam.

In the early 1950s the Trio Pim Jacobs came into being. It made its first LPs with, among others, Bud Shank, Bob Cooper, Tony Scott and Herbie Mann. In 1957 Ruud was chosen as the only bassist from Europe for the International Youth Band in the United States. There he played with, among others, Louis Armstrong. Afterwards he toured and recorded with, among others, Johnny Griffin, Kenny Clarke, Bud Powell, Bill Evans, Stan Getz, Sonny Rollins and Sarah Vaughan.

From the 1960s came the great successes with the singer Rita Reys, who in 1960 was proclaimed Europe's First Lady of Jazz at the Juan-les-Pins festival. The trio with the guitarist Wim Overgaauw played without a drummer, following the example of the Oscar Peterson trio. In this way Ruud Jacobs was part of the foundation of Dutch jazz on the international scene.
artiest/ruud-jacobs.listen: Listen to a recording of the Trio Pim Jacobs with Rita Reys and follow the double bass. Notice how Ruud Jacobs carries the rhythm without a drummer.

artiest/ry-cooder.text: Ry Cooder was born in Los Angeles in 1947 and was already playing the guitar at the age of three. He became known as a slide guitarist with a great interest in traditional music: blues, folk, gospel and music from other parts of the world. For the director Walter Hill he wrote, among others, the music for the western The Long Riders (1980), Southern Comfort (1981) and Crossroads (1986). His best-known score is Paris, Texas (1984) by Wim Wenders. Cooder based it on 'Dark Was the Night (Cold Was the Ground)' by the blues musician Blind Willie Johnson. In 1997 he produced the album Buena Vista Social Club with Cuban musicians. Wenders later made a documentary about it.
artiest/ry-cooder.listen: Listen to the slide guitar: the gliding notes, the sound that lingers, and the silences in between.

artiest/ryan-paris.text:
Ryan Paris is the stage name of the Italian singer and actor Fabio Roscioli, born in Rome in 1953. He grew up with music: a great-uncle was an opera singer. After a short career as an actor, with a small part in the film Once Upon a Time in America, he played in rock bands and a new wave group in Rome. When his band broke up in 1982 because members had to do military service, he came into contact, through the keyboard player of the group Stadio, with the producer and composer Pierluigi Giombini.

Giombini wrote and produced Dolce Vita for him. At first no record company wanted to release the song, but in the summer of 1983 it reached number 1 in the Netherlands, Flanders, France, Spain and the Scandinavian countries, and in England it made the top 5. After that Paris mostly had hits in southern Europe. In 1990 a remix by Ben Liebrand was released in the Netherlands.

Dolce Vita is a textbook example of Italo disco: an Italian studio production with synthesizers, a danceable rhythm and English-language vocals, made by a producer who went looking for a singer afterwards. The song continued to resonate. The Canadian indie musician Mac DeMarco cited Paris as an inspiration, and the two went on to record and perform together. In this way Ryan Paris is an example of an artist who became known mainly through a single song, which sums up an entire movement.
artiest/ryan-paris.listen: Listen to Dolce Vita and notice the bass: a synthesizer that bounces back and forth in fast, even eighth notes. Hear how that continuous bass line drives the song forward, while the vocals float calmly above it.

artiest/ryan-tedder.text:
Ryan Tedder is an American singer, musician, songwriter and producer, born in 1979. He grew up in a churchgoing family in Tulsa, Oklahoma, and learned to play the piano at the age of three. At seven he began to sing. He studied at Oral Roberts University, worked as an intern at DreamWorks in Nashville and made demos for other songwriters. He first gained recognition when he became a finalist in a singing competition on MTV. Afterwards he worked for several years with Timbaland.

Tedder is co-founder and lead singer of OneRepublic. His song Apologize became a worldwide hit. As a songwriter and producer he worked for many artists, including Leona Lewis, with Bleeding Love, and Beyoncé, with Halo. He also wrote for Kelly Clarkson, Adele, Taylor Swift, Ed Sheeran, Ariana Grande and Maroon 5. For his work on Adele's albums 21 and 25 and Taylor Swift's 1989 he received a Grammy for Album of the Year. In 2009 he started his own label and his own publishing company.

His songs are solidly built, and many in the business know his name only from the credits. Halo, from 2008, is a piano ballad that builds to a climax with choir, like a gospel song, which fits his churchgoing background. In 2014 Billboard called him the unseen king of pop. In the course he appears as one of the writers from the hit factory.
artiest/ryan-tedder.listen: Listen to Halo by Beyoncé and notice how the song begins with piano and voice. Can you hear how the choir joins in and the chorus keeps growing?

artiest/ryo-fukui.text:
Ryo Fukui was a Japanese jazz pianist from Sapporo, born in 1948 and died in 2016. He began on the accordion at eighteen and taught himself to play the piano at twenty-two. He then moved to Tokyo. The saxophonist Hidehiko Matsumoto gave him encouragement and advice, but Fukui often doubted his own progress. In the following years he often played in a trio with Satoshi Denpo and his brother Yoshinori Fukui, in clubs such as Shinjuku Pit Inn.

His first album, Scenery, was released in 1976, six years after his move to Tokyo. A year later came Mellow Dream. In 1992, during a trip to America, he met the pianist Barry Harris from Detroit, who became a friend and mentor and helped him with bebop. In 1994 My Favorite Tune was released, a solo album with his own work and arrangements of, among others, Sonny Clark. Four years later came In New York, with the drummer Leroy Williams and the bassist Lisle Atkinson. In 1995 he opened the jazz club Slowboat in Sapporo with his wife Yasuko, where he played regularly. He also taught and performed in France and America.

His playing is clear, infectious and full of swing, with a firm touch and a bluesy feeling that suits bebop. After his death his fame grew considerably. In the late 2010s Japanese jazz attracted renewed interest, above all with Scenery, which found a new audience through YouTube and streaming services. As a result collectors now hunt for his records, and reissues have appeared.
artiest/ryo-fukui.listen: Listen to Early Summer and notice the pianist, who makes a melody sing with a clear touch. Follow how the bass and drums make him swing and how every note is given space.

artiest/ryuichi-sakamoto.text: Ryuichi Sakamoto (1952–2023) studied composition at the Tokyo University of the Arts and became known with the electronic pop group Yellow Magic Orchestra. In Merry Christmas, Mr. Lawrence (1983) he played a role alongside David Bowie and also wrote the music. The title theme, a pentatonic melody with a synthesizer sound reminiscent of little bells, became world famous. For The Last Emperor (1987) he won an Oscar together with David Byrne and Cong Su. He combined romantic orchestral music, minimal music and electronics. Later he worked more and more with texture and noise, as in The Revenant (2015), together with Alva Noto.
artiest/ryuichi-sakamoto.listen: Notice the simple, repeated melody lying over shifting chords, and the combination of piano, strings and synthesizer.

artiest/rza.text:
RZA, real name Robert Fitzgerald Diggs, is an American rapper, producer, composer, actor and filmmaker, born in 1969 in Brownsville in Brooklyn. He came into contact with hip hop at the age of nine and was already taking part in rap battles at eleven. In the early 1980s he rapped with his cousins in small groups. In 1992 he founded the Wu-Tang Clan with his two cousins and five childhood friends, named after the kung fu film Shaolin and Wu Tang. He chose the name RZA himself.

In December 1992 the first single, Protect Ya Neck, was released, and in November 1993 the debut album Enter the Wu-Tang (36 Chambers). RZA was the de facto leader of the group, produced the tracks and decided who would be heard on which song. He also made almost everything for the other members' solo albums. In addition he was a member of Gravediggaz, under the name RZArector, and released solo records as Bobby Digital. He also wrote film music, including for Kill Bill, and directed The Man with the Iron Fists.

His production style revolves around soul samples, raw, sparse beats and cinematic sounds. His use of snippets from kung fu films gave the Wu-Tang Clan a world of its own. That influence carried through into much later hip hop. In the course he is the maker of the lo-fi beats beneath Protect Ya Neck, the song with which eight MCs from Staten Island announced themselves.
artiest/rza.listen: Listen to Protect Ya Neck and notice the raw, sober beat and the MCs who take turns. Can you hear the sample from a film in the sound?

artiest/s-d-burman.text: Sachin Dev Burman came from the royal family of Tripura and grew up with the folk music of Bengal. He first worked as a singer and composer in Calcutta and moved to Bombay in 1944. His songs are simple and melodious, often with Bengali folk melodies and light, airy accompaniment. He worked a great deal with Guru Dutt, for instance on Baazi (1951) and Pyaasa (1957), and with Dev Anand, including on Guide (1965). In Pyaasa, Mohammed Rafi sings the bitter Jinhe Naaz Hai Hind Par. With Aradhana (1969) and the singer Kishore Kumar he had another great success late in his career. His son R.D. Burman also became a film composer.
artiest/s-d-burman.listen: Notice the simple, folk-song-like melody and the light accompaniment, which gives the singer's voice all the space.

artiest/s-express.text:
S'Express was a British dance group from the late 1980s and early 1990s, centred on the DJ and producer Mark Moore. The project had one of the first commercial successes in acid house. Moore, who played in clubs a great deal, worked with a changing group of singers and musicians, including Pascal Gabriel, Jocasta, Mark D, Linda Love and Michellé. Later the group consisted only of Moore and the singer and DJ Sonique.

In April 1988 Theme from S'Express spent two weeks at the top of the British charts. The song contains elements of Is It Love You're After by Rose Royce and was among the first records to use the emerging sampling culture. It also made the American dance chart. The debut album Original Soundtrack was released in 1989, also featuring Superfly Guy and a version of Hey Music Lover by Sly and the Family Stone, a remix of whose B-side was made by the composer Philip Glass. The second album, Intercourse, was less successful but still produced club hits, such as Nothing to Lose. Sonique later had a career of her own and made It Feels So Good. Moore subsequently released records and remixes under his own name.

The music is cheerful and full of winks: a driving house beat, sampled bits of disco and soul, and vocals that sound like a party. The project showed how acid house, with sampling and DJ culture, found its way into British pop, and how such a style went straight into the charts.
artiest/s-express.listen: Listen to Theme from S'Express and notice the fragment of disco and soul worked into the song. Hear how that sampled fragment is mixed with a driving house beat into a dance track.

artiest/s-janaki.text:
Sistla Janaki was born in 1938 in a village in what is now Andhra Pradesh and died in 2026 in Mysuru. She was an Indian playback singer and occasional composer, affectionately called Janaki Amma and the Nightingale of South India. Her father was a doctor and teacher. She first performed at the age of nine and learned the basics of music from a nadaswaram player. On her uncle's advice she moved to Chennai, where she worked with the composer R. Sudarsanam at AVM Studios.

She began in 1957 with the Tamil film Vidhiyin Vilayattu and that same year already sang in six languages. Her mother tongue was Telugu, but she sang in about twenty languages, including Kannada, Tamil, Malayalam and Hindi. In total she recorded more than 48,000 songs for films, albums, television and radio, most of them in Kannada. In Telugu films she had hit after hit for years from 1957, until about the mid-1990s.

Her voice was praised for its expressiveness and modulation. She won four National Film Awards and 33 state awards. In 2013 she refused the Padma Bhushan because it came too late for her. In 2017 she bade farewell with a concert in Mysuru, with the Malayalam lullaby Amma Poovinum, although in 2018 she still sang for the Tamil film Pannaadi. In this way she sang for sixty years for virtually every major actress of South Indian cinema.
artiest/s-janaki.listen: Listen to Amma Poovinum and notice how softly and sensitively she sings the lullaby. Can you hear how she conveys emotion with small ornaments?

artiest/s-p-balasubrahmanyam.text:
Sripathi Panditaradhyula Balasubrahmanyam, known simply as SPB or Balu, was born in 1946 in Nellore in Andhra Pradesh and died in 2020. He was an Indian playback singer, presenter, actor, composer, voice actor and film producer. His father was a Harikatha storyteller and stage actor. Balu first wanted to become an engineer and went to the technical college in Anantapur, but music pulled harder. In 1964 he won an amateur singing competition in Madras. He led a light music group with, among others, Ilaiyaraaja and Gangai Amaran.

His debut as a playback singer was on 15 December 1966 in the Telugu film Sri Sri Sri Maryada Ramanna, with music by his mentor S. P. Kodandapani. He sang in films in Telugu, Tamil, Kannada, Malayalam and Hindi, in sixteen languages in total. He was regarded as one of the greatest singers of India.

He received the Padma Shri in 2001, the Padma Bhushan in 2011 and, after his death in 2021, the Padma Vibhushan. In 2016 he was named Indian Film Personality of the Year at the International Film Festival of India. His son S. P. Charan and his sister S. P. Sailaja are also singers. In 2025 a bronze statue of him was unveiled in Hyderabad. In this way he stands for the generation of singers who carried South Indian film music for decades.
artiest/s-p-balasubrahmanyam.listen: Find a Tamil or Telugu film song by S.P. Balasubrahmanyam and notice how he moves between power and softness with his voice. Can you hear that the song tells a story within the film?

artiest/s-u-r-v-i-v-e.text:
S U R V I V E, also written as Survive, is an American electronic band from Austin, Texas, founded in 2009. The members are Kyle Dixon, Michael Stein, Adam Jones and Mark Donica. Dixon and Stein compose and produce as a duo. The band makes synthesizer-heavy music influenced by horror film scores, with drum machines and analogue synthesizers.

The name became widely known when Dixon and Stein wrote the music for the Netflix series Stranger Things. The two volumes of the soundtrack, Music of Stranger Things, were each nominated for a Grammy in 2017, but did not win. In September 2017 they did receive an Emmy for the series' title music. Earlier the band had already contributed to the soundtrack of the horror film The Guest. In 2017 they also put together the music for Sensory, a restaurant experience at the Sugar Hill Mountain festival in Melbourne.

The band's own records carry cryptic titles, such as LT019 and s000 from 2011, HD009 and mnq026 from 2012 and RR7349 in 2016. The music evokes the 1980s, with pulsing bass lines and cool melodies. In this way the band showed that analogue synthesizers could reach a broad audience in the twenty-first century too.
artiest/s-u-r-v-i-v-e.listen: Listen to the main theme of Stranger Things and notice the pulsing synthesizer. Can you hear how few notes are enough for tension?

artiest/sabine-devieilhe.text:
Sabine Devieilhe was born in 1985 in Ifs, near Caen, into a family without professional musicians. She is a French coloratura soprano, known for her interpretations of Mozart, Baroque music and nineteenth-century opera. Critics often see her as the successor to Natalie Dessay. She began at the music school in Ifs and at the age of twelve went to the conservatoire in Caen to study the cello. Later she chose singing. She studied musicology and ethnomusicology in Rennes and sang in the chorus of the Opéra de Rennes. In 2008 she entered the Conservatoire de Paris.

In October 2011 she made her debut as a soloist at the Atelier Lyrique de Tourcoing as Amina in Bellini's La sonnambula. In 2012 followed Serpetta in La finta giardiniera in Aix-en-Provence and the title role in Lakmé in Montpellier. In 2013 she sang the Queen of the Night in Mozart's The Magic Flute for the first time, in Lyon, a role she later also sang at the Opéra Bastille in Paris and, in 2017, at the Royal Opera House in London. In 2013 she also sang Soeur Constance in Poulenc's Dialogues des Carmélites. In 2019 she made her debut at Carnegie Hall with French songs by Debussy and his circle.

In 2013 she became Révélation Artiste Lyrique and in 2015 Artiste lyrique de l'année at the Victoires de la musique classique. An asteroid bears her name. Her light, high voice and her agility make her one of the best-known French sopranos of her generation.
artiest/sabine-devieilhe.listen: Listen to an aria of the Queen of the Night from The Magic Flute in her performance. Notice the high notes and how precisely she sings the fast figures.

artiest/sabri-brothers-en-ensemble.text:
The Sabri Brothers were two brothers from Pakistan who, together with their ensemble, were among the greatest interpreters of Sufi qawwali. The group was led by Ghulam Farid Sabri and his younger brother Maqbool Ahmed Sabri. The band was originally founded by Maqbool when he was eleven, under the name Bacha Qawwal Party. His older brother Ghulam Farid joined at their father's insistence and became the leader, after which the group came to be called the Sabri Brothers. They were closely associated with the Chishti order, a Sufi brotherhood.

In qawwali a leader and a chorus sing religious poems, accompanied by harmonium, dholak and handclaps. The Sabri Brothers were called Shahanshah-e-Qawwali, the emperors of qawwali. They were the first qawwali performers to appear in the United States and other Western countries, and in 1975 the first Asian artists at Carnegie Hall in New York. Ghulam Farid died in 1994 and Maqbool led the group until his death in 2011, after which Mehmood Ghaznavi Sabri took over.

Their recordings were spread in the West mainly through albums such as Ya Habib from 1990 and Qawwali Masterworks from 1991. The music builds slowly: a calm beginning grows into a fierce, almost ecstatic repetition, in which the lead singer and the chorus drive each other on. In this way the brothers introduced an audience outside Pakistan to an age-old form of religious music.
artiest/sabri-brothers-en-ensemble.listen: Listen to Allah-hoo, Allah-hoo. Notice the repetition of the words, the alternation between solo voice and chorus, and how the tempo and tension slowly increase.

artiest/sabrina.text:
Sabrina Salerno, known as Sabrina, is an Italian singer, model, actress and television presenter, born in 1968. She grew up in Genoa and Sanremo and sang in the church choir as a child. After winning a beauty contest in Liguria she began as a model and made her television debut in 1984 in the programme Premiatissima. In 1986 her first single, Sexy Girl, was released, sung in English and produced by Claudio Cecchetto.

In 1987 came the album Sabrina and the single Boys (Summertime Love), which reached number 1 in France and Switzerland and number 3 in the United Kingdom. The video made her a sex symbol. After that came hits such as All of Me (Boy Oh Boy), produced by Stock Aitken Waterman, My Chico and Like a Yo-Yo, produced by Giorgio Moroder. In 1991 she sang the Italian-language Siamo donne with Jo Squillo at the Sanremo festival. In 1996 her first Italian album, Maschio dove sei, was released.

Sabrina made Euro disco and Italo: fast, tight dance music with striking visuals. With Boys (Summertime Love) she shows late Italo, already leaning almost towards Hi-NRG, as it sounded in the clubs. That is why she appears in the course as an example of 1980s dance music.
artiest/sabrina.listen: Listen to Boys (Summertime Love) and notice the fast, hard rhythm and the synthesizer line beneath the vocals. How clearly can you hear that this song was made for the dance floor?

artiest/sadao-watanabe.text: The alto saxophonist Sadao Watanabe was born in 1933 in Utsunomiya. In 1953 he joined Toshiko Akiyoshi's Cozy Quartet, which he took over when she left for America in 1956. Charlie Parker was his great example; in 1969 he dedicated a live record to him. From 1962 to 1965 he studied at Berklee in Boston and played with, among others, Chico Hamilton and Gary McFarland. Back in Tokyo he brought bossa nova and the Berklee theory with him and taught young musicians. At the end of the 1970s he became hugely popular in Japan with fusion records such as California Shower (1978).
artiest/sadao-watanabe.listen: Listen to the clear alto saxophone moving smoothly between bebop and bossa nova.

artiest/saint-louis-symphony-orchestra.text:
The Saint Louis Symphony Orchestra is an American symphony orchestra in St. Louis, Missouri. Joseph Otten founded it in 1880 as the St. Louis Choral Society. It is the second-oldest professional symphony orchestra in the United States; only the New York Philharmonic is older. Its regular concert hall is Powell Hall. In the 1881/82 season an orchestra of thirty-one members was added to the choir, and in 1893 the Choral-Symphony was formally established.

Its national reputation grew above all under the music director Leonard Slatkin, from 1979 to 1996. At that time the orchestra made many recordings for EMI and RCA Victor, toured Europe and the Far East and played at Carnegie Hall. Its finances could not keep up with that pace. After the departure of Hans Vonk, Itzhak Perlman was musical adviser from 2002 to 2004. From 2005 to 2018 David Robertson was music director. In 2005 a labour dispute led to two months without concerts. Under Robertson the orchestra went to the Proms in London for the first time in 2012, and since 2010 St. Louis Public Radio has broadcast the concerts live.

The orchestra recorded for labels including Columbia, RCA Victor, Telarc, Angel EMI and Nonesuch, and later for its own label, Arch Media. It received seven Grammys. It also sought a broader audience with popular-oriented series such as Live at Powell Hall.
artiest/saint-louis-symphony-orchestra.listen: Listen to a recording of the orchestra under Slatkin or Robertson and notice the full strings and the brass. Can you hear how the group plays as one whole?

artiest/salaam-remi.text:
Salaam Remi Gibbs was born in 1972 in Queens, New York, the son of a Trinidadian mother and a Barbadian father, the studio musician Van Joseph Gibbs. As a keyboard player he first appeared on a record in 1986, Kingdom Blow by Kurtis Blow. In the late 1980s he began mixing records. His first complete production was in 1992 for the hip hop group Zhigge. After that he worked with the Fugees and Black Sheep.

He produced for, among others, Nas, Amy Winehouse and Jazmine Sullivan, and also for Alicia Keys, Doja Cat, Miguel and Nelly Furtado. He contributed to The Score by the Fugees and to Here Comes the Hotstepper by Ini Kamoze. For Ms. Dynamite he made ten tracks on A Little Deeper from 2002, including the successful Dy-Na-Mi-Tee. For Amy Winehouse he did tracks on Frank, her debut, and on Back to Black, and he worked on her third album until her death. He is known for his reggae-tinged approach to production, often called broken-bottle.

He has also worked on film music, including for Office Space, Zoolander and The Departed. In 2013 he started his label Louder Than Life at Sony. After ten Grammy nominations he won a Grammy in 2021 for the soundtrack of The United States vs. Billie Holiday. As a producer he often works in the background, but he helps determine the sound of records.
artiest/salaam-remi.listen: Listen to a track by Amy Winehouse from Frank or Back to Black and notice the drums, the bass and the horns. Can you hear how the production links old soul with a modern beat?

artiest/salt-n-pepa.text:
Salt-N-Pepa is an American hip hop group from New York, formed in 1985, with Salt (Cheryl James), Pepa (Sandra Denton) and DJ Spinderella. The two women met at the department store Sears and were studying nursing. Their colleague Hurby Azor, who was studying music production, wrote The Showstopper for them. After that they dropped out of their studies. Azor came up with the name Salt-N-Pepa from the lyrics of that song.

The debut album Hot, Cool & Vicious from 1986 sold more than a million copies in the United States. They were the first female rap group to go both gold and platinum. The big success came when DJ Cameron Paul remixed the B-side Push It. After that followed A Salt with a Deadly Pepa in 1988, Blacks' Magic in 1990 with Expression and Let's Talk About Sex, and Very Necessary in 1993 with Shoop, which sold more than five million copies in the United States. Brand New appeared later, in 1997.

The group emerged at a time when hip hop was considered a passing fad. It made cheerful, danceable rap with lyrics about women, self-confidence and sex, and so offered a counterweight to sexist lyrics and videos. It sold more than fifteen million records and was given the title The First Ladies of Rap.
artiest/salt-n-pepa.listen: Listen to Push It and notice the drum machine and the short rap lines. Can you hear how the two voices take turns?

artiest/sam-cooke.text:
Sam Cooke, born Samuel Cook in 1931 in Clarksdale, Mississippi, was an American soul singer and songwriter. He was the son of a Baptist minister and grew up in Chicago. At the age of six he sang in a little group with his brothers and sisters, and as a teenager he became the singer of the Highway Q.C.'s. In 1950 he replaced R.H. Harris in the gospel group The Soul Stirrers. His young, supple voice drew mostly young girls to the concerts.

In 1956 he left the Soul Stirrers for a career in popular music. That drew criticism from the gospel world. He first recorded his first pop song under another name and in 1958 added an e to his surname. In his career of thirteen years he had twenty-nine singles in the American top forty. In 1964 came A Change Is Gonna Come, a song that became a symbol of the civil rights movement. At the end of 1964 he was shot dead in a motel in Los Angeles. His family has doubted the official account ever since.

Cooke brought the singing of gospel into popular music and is often called the King of Soul. In 2015 Rolling Stone ranked him third among the greatest singers of all time. In the course he is the example of a singer from gospel who gave a voice to the struggle for equal rights.
artiest/sam-cooke.listen: Listen to A Change Is Gonna Come and notice how his voice begins, calm and almost soft, and then grows stronger. Can you hear the gospel in the way he sings the lines?

artiest/sam-en-dave.text:
Sam & Dave was an American soul duo of Sam Moore and Dave Prater. Both grew up with gospel at home and in church. In 1961 they met at the King of Hearts nightclub in Miami, where Moore was hosting an amateur night. When Prater lost the words of a Jackie Wilson song, Moore jumped in. From that evening they sang together. Their first singles, on small labels and on Roulette in New York, did not yet break through.

In 1964 Jerry Wexler signed the duo to Atlantic. He lent them out to Stax in Memphis, because he wanted to capture on record the southern gospel sound of their live shows. There Isaac Hayes and David Porter wrote and produced the great hits: You Don't Know Like I Know and Hold On, I'm Comin' (1966), the ballad When Something Is Wrong with My Baby (1967), Soul Man (1967) and I Thank You (1968). Booker T. & the M.G.'s and the horns of The Mar-Keys played on them. When the deal between Atlantic and Stax ran out in 1968, the duo lost its writers and musicians, and the hits dried up.

The strength of Sam & Dave was the call-and-response singing of the Black church: Moore sang the high voice, Prater the lower one, and they answered each other like preacher and congregation. On stage they were so energetic that they earned the nickname Double Dynamite. Soul Man helped establish the word soul as the name of a genre. In the late 1970s the cover by The Blues Brothers brought the duo renewed attention.
artiest/sam-en-dave.listen: Listen to Soul Man and notice how Sam and Dave alternate and complement each other, with the horns adding short bursts in between. Hear how the Stax house band gives the singers room.

artiest/sam-jones.text:
Sam Jones was an American jazz bassist, cellist and composer. He was born in 1924 in Jacksonville, Florida, into a musical family: his father played piano and drums, his aunt the organ in church. At school he began on drums in a brass band and later switched to the double bass. In the mid-1950s he moved to New York, where he worked with, among others, Kenny Dorham, Illinois Jacquet, Bill Evans, Dizzy Gillespie and Thelonious Monk.

Internationally he became known mainly as the bassist in Cannonball Adderley's quintet, which he joined around 1959 and in which he played until the mid-1960s. Many of those recordings were released on Riverside Records. Afterwards he played in the Oscar Peterson trio from 1966 to 1970 and in the 1970s with Cedar Walton. As a leader he made records for Xanadu and SteepleChase, such as Visitation from 1978. Two of his compositions from the Adderley years, Del Sasser and Unit 7, have become jazz standards.

Jones was the kind of bassist who carries the ensemble without drawing attention to himself. Playing with drummers such as Louis Hayes and Billy Higgins, he formed a rhythm section that gave soloists all the room they needed. He also played the cello, which is rare in jazz, and belonged to Bill Lee's New York Bass Violin Choir. He died in 1981 of lung cancer. Anyone who listens to the hard bop of the 1950s and 1960s will almost always hear his bass beneath the best recordings.
artiest/sam-jones.listen: Listen to The Soul Society from 1960 and pay attention only to the double bass. Can you hear how the bass keeps a steady, warm pulse while the horns solo?

artiest/sam-musiker.text:
Sam Musiker was an American clarinettist and saxophonist who worked in both jazz and klezmer. He was born in New York in 1916 and lived there for most of his life. His field of work was broad: he played in bars, restaurants and recording studios among swing musicians, but also at weddings and in the hotels of the Jewish music world outside the city.

In 1938 he was there at the founding of Gene Krupa's orchestra, after Krupa had left Benny Goodman. He stayed until 1944 and soloed on several recordings. He also played with Glenn Miller and recorded with Sarah Vaughan. During the war he led an Air Force band. Later he moved to Tucson, Arizona, where he taught and wrote arrangements.

His best-known work is the album Tanz, recorded in 1955 and released a year later. It was an attempt to combine klezmer with big band swing. Musiker led the project, with his brother Ray Musiker and his father-in-law, the clarinettist Dave Tarras. The rhythm was lively, with bass on the beat and piano or accordion on the offbeat. The record sold poorly at first, but is now regarded as a milestone of Jewish-American music. Musiker formed a link between the klezmer of Eastern Europe and the American sound of New York. He died in 1964.
artiest/sam-musiker.listen: Listen to a track from Tanz and try to hear the two worlds: the clarinet that weeps and rejoices as in klezmer, and beneath it the swinging rhythm section of a big band.

artiest/sam-phillips.text:
Sam Phillips was an American record producer from Memphis, Tennessee. In his Memphis Recording Service he recorded Black blues and rhythm and blues musicians in the early 1950s and founded the label Sun Records. His studio was open to musicians who could not get a foothold with the major labels.

Phillips's name is above all linked to Elvis Presley, who made his first records with him at Sun in 1954. After that Johnny Cash, Carl Perkins, Jerry Lee Lewis and Roy Orbison also came to Sun. Orbison signed in 1956, at the urging of Johnny Cash, when Presley left Sun and Phillips was looking for a replacement. Phillips was known for his raw, direct recording sound, with plenty of echo and little polish, and for his ability to let musicians be themselves.

In a small studio in Memphis Phillips laid the foundation for rock 'n' roll and rockabilly. In the course he appears as the man at whose studio a song was recorded a few years before he would discover Elvis. He is not the same person as the singer of the same name from California.
artiest/sam-phillips.listen: Listen to an early Sun recording by Elvis Presley, such as That's All Right, and notice the echo on the voice and the simple accompaniment. Can you hear how raw and direct the sound is?

artiest/sam-rivers.text:
Sam Rivers was an American jazz musician and composer. He was born in 1923 in El Reno, Oklahoma, the son of a gospel singer. He played tenor and soprano saxophone, bass clarinet, flute, harmonica, piano and viola. In 1947 he moved to Boston, where he studied at the conservatory and played with, among others, Quincy Jones and Tadd Dameron.

In 1964 he briefly played in Miles Davis's quintet, which recorded a live album in Tokyo. His style proved too adventurous for Davis. He then signed with Blue Note and recorded four albums as a leader, including Fuchsia Swing Song from 1964 and A New Conception from 1967. On them he played an approach sometimes called inside-outside: he left the chord changes, but kept a hidden bond with them. His ballad Beatrice became a standard for tenor saxophonists.

In the 1970s he ran the loft Studio Rivbea in New York with his wife Beatrice, the best-known venue for loft jazz. Musicians made their own stage there and were not dependent on clubs. In those years he recorded for Impulse!, for instance Crystals with his first big band. Later he lived in Florida, where his RivBea Orchestra kept playing. He died in 2011. Rivers shows that free jazz and bebop can lie close together.
artiest/sam-rivers.listen: Listen to Fuchsia Swing Song from 1964 and notice the moments when the saxophone lets go of the chord changes and yet returns to them.

artiest/sam-wooding.text:
Sam Wooding was an American jazz pianist, arranger and bandleader. He was born in 1895 in Philadelphia, the son of a butler. He taught himself to play the piano, wrote his first composition as a child and became a professional musician around 1910. In the First World War he served in an army band led by the Broadway arranger Will Vodery.

After the war he played in Atlantic City and, from 1920, in Harlem, with a group of his own. In 1922 he made his first recordings, including under the name of Johnny Dunn's Original Jazz Hounds. His great breakthrough came in 1925, when his orchestra went to Europe as part of the revue Chocolate Kiddies. They played in Berlin, Hamburg, Stockholm and Copenhagen and recorded in Berlin for the label Vox. Tours of Russia followed, in 1927 of Argentina, and around 1929 once more of Europe, with recordings in Barcelona and Paris.

His orchestra was the first Black orchestra to tour Europe extensively and to make recordings there. In Argentina audiences got to know a jazz that was more syncopated and more centred on improvisation than the ragtime before it. Wooding even played a melody by Wagner in jazz form. He returned to the United States in 1934, studied music and taught, among others Clifford Brown. He died in 1985 in Manhattan.
artiest/sam-wooding.listen: Listen to a recording by Sam Wooding from the 1920s and notice how the orchestra sounds: firmly arranged, with a brisk rhythm and short solos, still close to the dance music of that time.

artiest/samara-joy.text: Samara Joy McLendon grew up in the Bronx in a family of gospel singers. She discovered jazz only during her studies and in 2019 won the Sarah Vaughan International Jazz Vocal Competition. Sarah Vaughan and Ella Fitzgerald are her most important role models. Her warm, rich voice and classic repertoire from the Great American Songbook brought her a large, young audience through social media. In 2023 she won the Grammy for Best New Artist, as the second jazz musician after Esperanza Spalding. On Portrait (2024) she sings with an octet of her own.
artiest/samara-joy.listen: Listen to the deep, round sound and the long, calm lines of the voice.

artiest/sammy-price.text:
Sammy Price, in full Samuel Blythe Price, was an American jazz, boogie-woogie and jump blues pianist and bandleader, born in 1908 in Honey Grove, Texas. He received formal piano lessons from Portia Marshall Washington, the daughter of Booker T. Washington. In the mid-1920s he worked in a music shop in Dallas and wrote to Paramount Records to recommend Blind Lemon Jefferson. He played and sang in clubs around Dallas and later lived and worked in Kansas City, Chicago and Detroit.

In 1938 Decca Records hired him as a session pianist. He accompanied, among others, Trixie Smith and Sister Rosetta Tharpe, and his trio played with Tharpe and Marie Knight on gospel recordings such as Up Above My Head. With his own group, the Texas Bluesicians, he also recorded for Decca. His playing is dark, mellow and relaxed, not rhythmically hard, and on blues recordings he knew exactly how to strike the right mood and swing. He recorded with Lester Young, toured Europe with Jimmy Rushing and played in a Broadway play with Tallulah Bankhead. From 1943 he played at the Café Society Uptown in New York, sometimes on the same bill as Art Tatum.

Price was one of the pianists behind the female singers of the 1940s. In the course he appears in the chapter on women in popular music as the pianist who recorded Strange Things Happening Every Day with Rosetta Tharpe in 1944.
artiest/sammy-price.listen: Listen to Strange Things Happening Every Day and notice the piano beneath the voice. How does Price give the rhythm momentum and at the same time leave room for the voice?

artiest/samuel-barber.text:
Samuel Barber was an American composer, pianist, conductor, baritone and music teacher, born in 1910 and died in 1981. He studied composition for nine years with Rosario Scalero at the Curtis Institute and for more than twenty-five years with his uncle, the composer Sidney Homer. His work was for a long time very popular and he was regarded as one of the best-known composers of the mid-twentieth century.

Barber remained largely faithful to the traditional harmony and form of the nineteenth century. His music is lyrical and emotional. His Adagio for Strings from 1936 is firmly established in the orchestral repertoire, as is the choral version, Agnus Dei from 1967. He twice won the Pulitzer Prize for Music, for the opera Vanessa and for the Concerto for Piano and Orchestra. Knoxville: Summer of 1915 is also widely performed. Two thirds of his work consists of vocal music: songs with piano, choral music and songs with orchestra, such as Sure on this shining night and the cycle Hermit Songs. This stems from his own short career as a baritone.

The Adagio is a slow piece for strings that builds gradually and ends in a climax. That made it suited to a new life in dance music, when Tiësto turned it into a trance hit in 2004. In the course this appears as a listening tip.
artiest/samuel-barber.listen: Listen to Tiësto's Adagio for Strings and notice the build-up: Barber's melody, the break and then the release. Compare that with the original string piece from 1936.

artiest/samuel-e-wright.text:
Samuel E. Wright was an American actor, voice actor and singer. He was born in 1946 in Camden, South Carolina, and moved to New York in 1968 to work as an actor. He worked mainly in the theatre: on Broadway he took over the role of Leading Player in Pippin from Ben Vereen and appeared in Over Here!. In 1984 he was nominated for a Tony Award for The Tap Dance Kid. In 1998 came a second nomination, as the first Mufasa in the Broadway version of The Lion King.

His best-known work is the voice of Sebastian, the crab in the Disney film The Little Mermaid from 1989. He sang the lead part of Under the Sea, which won the Oscar for best original song, and also Kiss the Girl. He voiced Sebastian again in the sequels and series, up to and including The Little Mermaid: Ariel's Beginning. He also voiced Kron in the film Dinosaur from 2000. In 1988 he played the trumpeter Dizzy Gillespie in Bird, Clint Eastwood's film about Charlie Parker, and he was the narrator of the documentary Thelonious Monk: Straight, No Chaser. For the record company he also made albums in a reggae style, including Sebastian Party Gras!.

Under the Sea shows the reggae and calypso that characterise Sebastian: a light rhythm section, steel drums and a playful, singing voice. Wright showed that a voice actor with real singing power can turn a supporting part in an animated film into a hit. He died in 2021 in Walden, New York.
artiest/samuel-e-wright.listen: Listen to Under the Sea and notice the rhythm, which resembles calypso and reggae, and the way Wright makes his voice dance. Can you hear how the song slowly grows bigger, with more and more voices and instruments?

artiest/samuel-hoffman.text:
Samuel Hoffman was an American theremin player, born in 1903 in New York. At the age of fourteen he was already playing the violin professionally and leading nightclub and society orchestras under the stage name Hal Hope. In the early 1930s he received an RCA theremin from 1929 as payment of a debt. In 1936 he had a nine-piece swing orchestra in which he played both violin and theremin. Later he became a podiatrist and in 1941 moved his practice to Los Angeles. That is why he was often called Doctor.

His big moment came in 1944, when the composer Miklos Rozsa wanted a theremin in the film music for Alfred Hitchcock's Spellbound. Hoffman turned out to be the only thereminist in the musicians' union register who could read music. The score won an Oscar. After that he played on the music for The Lost Weekend, The Spiral Staircase and later on science fiction films such as The Day The Earth Stood Still. That music was also used as the title theme of Lost in Space.

With the bandleader Les Baxter and Harry Revel he recorded Music Out of the Moon in 1947, according to the source the best-selling theremin record ever. The sequel Perfume Set to Music from 1948 reached first place on the Variety chart, and in 1950 followed Music For Peace Of Mind. These records are regarded as precursors of exotica and space age pop. Sun Ra recorded a piece of it for his first album. One of Hoffman's last recordings was Safe as Milk by Captain Beefheart. He died in 1967.
artiest/samuel-hoffman.listen: Listen to Music Out of the Moon and notice the sound of the theremin: a floating, almost singing tone that seems to glide through the air without a string or key involved.

artiest/samuel-scheidt.text:
Samuel Scheidt was a German composer, organist and teacher of the early Baroque. He was baptised in 1587 in Halle and died there in 1654. His parents belonged to the town's prominent circles and all three sons became organists. Samuel was the most important of the three. As early as 1603 he was organist at the Moritzkirche. In 1607 and 1608 he studied in Amsterdam with Jan Pieterszoon Sweelinck, whose style can clearly be heard in his work.

Back in Halle he became court organist and later Kapellmeister to the Margrave of Brandenburg. Unlike many German musicians, he stayed in Germany during the Thirty Years' War. He kept going by teaching and with smaller jobs. When he lost his post with the margrave in 1628, he became musical director of three churches in Halle, including the Marktkirche. In 1624 his Tabulatura nova was published, a collection of organ music that is still published and recorded today.

His work falls into two groups: instrumental music, mainly for organ, and sacred vocal music, sometimes a cappella, sometimes with basso continuo. In his chorale settings he often used variation technique: each line of the chorale was given its own rhythmic motif and each variation became richer than the last, up to the climax. He also wrote fugues, dance suites and fantasias. Scheidt is regarded as the first German organ composer of international significance and as a representative of the new North German style that emerged after the Reformation.
artiest/samuel-scheidt.listen: Listen to a part of Tabulatura nova on organ. Try to hear how the same melody keeps coming back, each time with a different rhythm and richer ornamentation.
